frameworks.name: Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate
frameworks.definition: A three-step training method for transferring procedural knowledge: document the exact steps of a process while performing it, demonstrate the process by executing steps with explanation, then have the learner duplicate the process under observation until mastery.

frameworks.name: Declarative vs. Procedural Knowledge
frameworks.definition: Two distinct types of learnable knowledge: declarative knowledge (knowing that something exists, the unknown unknowns) versus procedural knowledge (knowing how to execute a task step-by-step).

claims.text: There are two types of learnable knowledge: declarative knowledge (learning about things that exist) and procedural knowledge (learning how to do things). Declarative knowledge teaches unknown unknowns—breakthrough insights from exposure to strategies and business models you haven't encountered. Procedural knowledge is more predictable because you already know the thing exists and only need to clarify the execution steps.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: When investing time, money, or relational capital into learning (via coaching, networks, or training), you must delineate what you are actually buying: declarative knowledge (exposure to unknowns) or procedural knowledge (execution steps). Failure to specify what you're learning leads to incomplete learning and wasted investment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any learning investment: time, money, or relational capital
Access to networks, coaches, or educational programs
claims.mechanism: Declaring what you are buying prevents false expectations and allows you to optimize for the correct knowledge type.

claims.text: Declarative knowledge is most valuable when obtained from people operating at 10-100x your current performance level, because their worldview and available mental models differ fundamentally from yours.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Seeking to expand knowledge of business models or strategies
Access to high-performing peers or mentors
claims.mechanism: High performers see the world differently and hold knowledge of unexposed opportunities; exposure to their models creates access to new possibility spaces.

claims.text: Procedural knowledge mastery via the Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate method requires multiple iterations (Hormozi's ad-scaling example: 8 sessions) and is complete when the learner can execute steps correctly without correction from the instructor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Teaching a specific procedure or skill
Access to instructor for demonstration and feedback
claims.mechanism: Sequential exposure to the process (documentation + demonstration + replication) encodes procedural knowledge through observation and repeated execution; correction loops tighten until error-free replication occurs.
bounded_by: Requires learner willingness to practice under observation
Requires instructor availability for multiple sessions

claims.text: Relational capital is finite; asking for help repeatedly without reciprocal investment depletes trust and access. Once relational capital is exhausted, even low-cost alternatives (e.g., $7.50/hour labor) become viable negotiation paths.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Repeatedly seeking help from networks or contacts
Operating without reciprocal value to offer
claims.mechanism: Relationships are transactional at scale; repeated asks without exchange reduce the asker's credibility and willingness of contact to engage.
bounded_by: Does not apply to immediate family or formal mentorship relationships with explicit give-to-ask ratios

claims.text: Preparation and structured learning discipline (pre-call notes, recordings, multiple observers, repeated verification of correct execution) compensate for paying below-market rates for instruction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Learning procedural knowledge from a paid instructor
Instructor rates are below-market due to unconventional payment structure (hourly vs retainer)
claims.mechanism: High-effort learner preparation and documentation discipline extract maximum value from limited instructor time, making lower-cost arrangements economically viable.

examples.text: In 2013, Hormozi learned that Facebook ads existed and within one weekend self-taught the mechanics well enough to operate them profitably. This illustrates rapid mastery of procedural knowledge when declarative knowledge (ad existence and basic structure) was already known. He then operated this skill set for several years before needing to scale from local to national campaigns.

To scale Facebook ad operations nationally, Hormozi needed procedural knowledge beyond his local-ads expertise. He called agencies quoting $5,000/month; he couldn't afford this rate. He negotiated a $7.50/hour arrangement with an experienced practitioner. Over 8 one-hour sessions, Hormozi applied the Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate method: the instructor documented his ad-management process step-by-step, demonstrated each step with explanation, and Hormozi replicated in real-time under observation until error-free execution. Hormozi prepared heavily for each call (notes, recorder, two additional observers) to extract maximum value from the low-cost arrangement. This sequence took 8 hours total and taught him to run ads at national scale.

practices.text: When investing in learning, always clarify upfront whether you are buying declarative knowledge (exposure to unknowns and new mental models) or procedural knowledge (execution steps for a known task).

If learning procedural knowledge at a reduced rate, commit to maximum preparation discipline: pre-call research, detailed note-taking, recordings, and having multiple observers present to ensure knowledge transfer.
Master a procedural skill only when you can execute the steps correctly and repeatedly without instructor correction.
